title: ♾️ CICD Explained for Dummies! CICD Pipeline in 60 seconds #devops #cicd
text: what is cicd cicd is a process to automate the building testing and deploying of applications every time you make a code change so that you can update and deliver your applications faster let's understand this more clearly with a diagram whenever a developer makes some changes and pushes it to get repository like GitHub an automated CI server like genkins will continuously monitor this repository for any new code changes and if they detected it triggers the pipeline which automatically builds and tests the code every time you make a change this process of automatically building and testing the codee is known as continuous integration once the code is built and test it is then ready for the next part which is the deployment part you can deploy your applications either on kubernetes or on servers and this complete process is known as cicd pipeline for more information on Hands-On cicd projects check out the videos on my channel

title: AWS Certification Roadmap in 2025! ☁️ #aws #cloud
text: AWS has 12 different certifications, but if you are confused which certification to start with, ask yourself a question. How much experience do I have in the cloud? If you have no experience or a complete beginner, the best certification to start with is the AWS Cloud Practitioner. AWS Cloud Practitioner is a foundational level certification specific for beginners in the cloud. But if you have experience working on AWS, you can start with role-specific certification like the Solutions Architect Associate or Developer Associate or maybe other certifications like DevOps Professional, Security Specialty, Networking, etc. In short, if you are a complete beginner, start with AWS Cloud Practitioner, or else you can go for Associate level certifications or maybe Specialty certification and even Professional level certifications. To learn more about cloud and DevOps, subscribe to Cloud Chat.

title: Ansible : The Automation tool ♾️ | How does Ansible work? 💭🤔 #ansible #devops
text: Hey, DevOps engineers. Have you ever wished you could automate all the repetitive tasks that you do every day? Well, with Ansible you can. Ansible is an open source configuration management tool used to automate infrastructure management and configuration. Using Ansible, you can configure hundreds and thousands of servers with just a single command. So, how does Ansible work? Ansible uses something known as playbook written in YAML syntax, where you can define all your task and configurations that you want to be applied on all the servers. Along with the playbook, you also need a host file or inventory file, which will contain the IP addresses of all the servers on which you want to run the playbook. After you have the playbook and define your servers in the host file, you can run the Ansible command, which will run this playbook on all the servers defined in the host file using SSH. This is how Ansible can be used to manage and configure multiple servers at once.

title: Observability Explained Simply in 60 seconds #observability #devops
text: What is observability? Observability is a way to find out what's happening inside a complex system. Modern apps run across many services, APIs, and containers. So when something breaks, you depend on three core signals: metrics, logs, and traces. Metrics are numbers that reflect system health like CPU, latency, throughput, memory, etc. Logs are detailed event messages that tell you exactly what happened and why. And lastly, traces show you the complete path a request takes across multiple services to know where the request failed or slowed down. When you bring metrics, logs, and traces together, observability can help you answer critical questions like where did the request fail? Which microservices is causing slowdown? Is the issue in code infrastructure or any other dependency and many other questions. So in short, observability helps engineers debug faster and understand system behavior more clearly whenever there's an issue. Subscribe.

title: All HTTP status codes Explained! #shorts #http
text: let's understand HTTP status codes HTTP or hypertext transfer protocol is used for communication between client and a server on the internet when you make an API call the response returns a three-digit status code which helps us understand the outcome of the request status codes in 1xx range are informational and indicate that the request has been received and the process is continuing status codes in 2xx range are successful and it means that the request has been received understood and accepted status code with 3xx range means redirection this is usually because the requested resource has moved to a different URL status code in 4xx range indicates an issue with the client's request such as invalid request or unauthorized access and lastly status code with 5xx range indicates the server issue where a server failed to fulfill a valid request due to internal issues

title: Kubernetes Cluster Multitenancy Explained in 50 seconds! #vcluster
text: Imagine your company has five teams, front end, back end, ML, QA, and DevOps. All of them sharing the same Kubernetes cluster to run their application. But there's a problem. One team is using too much CPU or power. Another team's pod is talking to the wrong services. And then security becomes a concern. What these teams really need is a separate isolated environment, fair resource sharing, and secure access. And that's where Kubernetes multi-tenency comes into play. Multi-tenency means letting multiple projects or teams use the same cluster to run workloads keeping them safe and separated. You can do this using name spaces to separate workloads, arbback to secure access, resource kas to limit how much CPU and memory can be used. But if you need more isolation, you can also try out virtual clusters by vclusters or dedicated clusters as well. Subscribe.

title: How Work IQ Reasons Across Microsoft 365 Apps!
text: MCP is everywhere. Let me show you a real enterprise example. So, this is a demo environment containing emails, team messages, meetings, documents, and calendars. I asked Microsoft Work IQ one question. What are Monica Thompson's current commitment and can she take on a new customer? Now, think about that question for a second. This information is not present in a single application. Some information might be in her Outlook mails or Teams chat. title: AI Pipeline Explained! How Ai pipeline works? #ai
text: What is AI pipeline and how does it work? Just like how CICD pipeline turns code into a deployed application in DevOps, an AI pipeline is a process that turns raw data into a working AI feature in production. So, here's how it works. It starts with data collection where data is gathered from different sources like databases, APIs, or logs. This data is then cleaned and prepared so the model can learn from it properly. Next, an AI model is trained on this data to learn patterns or make predictions. After training, the model is evaluated using metrics like accuracy and precision to make sure it performs well. If it passes the accuracy threshold, the model is then deployed into production to make predictions. After deployment, monitoring will track the performance of your model detecting issues like performance drop or data drift. In short, this feedback of the AI pipeline is super important to retrain or improve the model over time making the pipeline continuous just like CICD pipeline. Subscribe.

text: Terafform versus Ansible. What is the difference? Hashikorp Terapform is an infrastructure as code tool used to create cloud infrastructures like servers, databases, network, storage, etc. Once the infrastructure is created, you can configure them using configuration management tool like anible. So, Ansible is a configuration management tool that can be used to install software, start, stop services, manage configuration files and lot more. In short, Teraphform is used to create infrastructure. Anible is used to configure it. For example, a DevOps engineer will use Terapform to create EC2 instance in the cloud and then use Ansible to install and configure EngineX server on that EC2 instance created by Terapform.

title: What is OpenTelemetry & How Otel works? #otel
text: What is open telemetry? Open telemetry is an open source standard for collecting logs, metrics, and traces from your application. So, instead of using different libraries or tools for each type of telemetry data, OpenTelemetry provides you with a unified way to generate and send all observability data. And here's how it works. OpenTelemetry provides with instrumentation libraries for languages like Golang, Java, Python, and Node.js that automatically captures key events like HTTP calls, database queries, or service-to-service communication. >> The most important component is the OpenTelemetry Collector, which receives telemetry data from your applications and forwards it to any back end you choose. Could be Honeycomb, Datadog, New Relic, Jaeger, Grafana, anything. And because OpenTelemetry uses a common protocol, OLTP, all the telemetry data is consistent and vendor neutral. So, in short, OpenTelemetry is an open source tool that helps you understand what your app is doing by collecting logs, metrics, and traces, and sending this data to any observability tool, so you can understand what's the issue and fix it. title: RAG vs Fine Tuning Simply Explained!
text: RAG and fine-tuning are two completely different concepts. Let me explain. With RAG or retrieval augmented generation, we give AI access to external knowledge. Usually, this means taking documents, PDFs, websites, and converting them into embeddings, storing them in a vector database, and then retrieving the most relevant information whenever a user asks a question. But, fine-tuning is different. Fine-tuning is not about giving model knowledge, it's about changing how the model behaves. So, you take a base model like 4.1 and then train it further using example prompts or ideal responses. The result is a specialized model that learns your tone, your format, writing style, or output structure. For example, if you want AI chatbot to answer questions based on your company documents, use RAG. But, if you want AI to sound exactly like your brand or answer question in a specific format, use fine-tuning. Subscribe.

title: Generative AI vs AI Agents vs Agentic AI Explained Simply with Example in 5 Mins!
text: Hi everyone, in this video you will understand the clear difference between Gen AI, AI agents and agentic AI with a real world example. Understanding the difference between these three is super important for anyone learning or using AI tools. So make sure you like this video and watch it till the end. Let's imagine you work in a company as a DevOps engineer and you are given a task to migrate a microservices application from virtual machine to Kubernetes by creating health charts, deploying services, implementing, monitoring and also resolving if any issues arise. Now this task is a complex task that requires thinking, planning, writing code, running commands, debugging and also validating if the migration is successful or not. Using this example, let's understand how Gen AI or AI agents or agentic AI would handle this task and through this the difference will become very clear. Let's start with Gen AI. So Gen AI or generative AI is a type of artificial intelligence that is trained on huge massive data sets to generate

title: Generative AI vs AI Agents vs Agentic AI Explained Simply with Example in 5 Mins!
text: new content like text, images, music, videos, etc. Responding to simple human prompts. For example, these are all the popular geni tools used in the market. Everyone knows about chat GPT and Claude. If you are a software engineer, you also know about GitHub copilot. If you're a designer, you might use Dolly or Canva AI as well. Popular Gen AI models like GPT4 or Claude is used by software engineers to create code, documentation, even explanations. But the problem is Gen AI can create content. It cannot perform actual task or it cannot interact with the systems. What do I mean is for example if I give the same migration task to chat GPT asking it to help me out it will generate helm charts yl configuration it will also create kubernetes manifest files for deployment it will explain me all the best practices for migration but it cannot build the image it cannot connect to the cluster it cannot run the commands for me or it cannot verify if everything is done or not so this is the

title: Generative AI vs AI Agents vs Agentic AI Explained Simply with Example in 5 Mins!
text: flow when working with genai you will ask what you want and it will generate the content for you but you have to implement it you have to run the command you will also have to fix if there are any issues. So these Gen AI tools are smart but they don't plan, they cannot use APIs, they cannot execute workflows on their own. You have to do it as a user. Now let's talk about AI agents. AI agents are built on top of Gen AI. But they also have ability to use tools, call APIs, execute commands and also interact with system. Which means unlike Gen AI which can only create content, AI agents can create content and also take actions on your behalf. So if I give the same migration example to an AI agent created maybe using N10. So it will generate all the code and the manifest file required for migration through GNI capabilities and then also connect to your cluster using the cubernetes API and your credentials. Next, it will run

title: Generative AI vs AI Agents vs Agentic AI Explained Simply with Example in 5 Mins!
text: the commands to apply all the changes, verify if everything is working properly and also notify you using Slack API. This means AI agents are able to understand the prompt given by the user also decide what steps to take and actually take actions on your behalf. But the problem with AI agents are they are mostly used for single task that once the task is done AI agents will stop and that's why using AI agents for long or complex task is not the right choice. So you should use agentic AI. Agentic AI is more advanced and takes the AI agent concept further by being fully autonomous which means agentic AI can work without user instructions for hours or even for days until the task is achieved. It also uses multi-step planning by understanding the complete goal and breaking them into small pieces. It has long-term memory also selfcorrection which means if there are any issues agentic AI will solve it. Now unlike AI agent rather than following stepby-step instruction agentic AI operates like a self-managed DevOps team

title: Generative AI vs AI Agents vs Agentic AI Explained Simply with Example in 5 Mins!
text: understanding the complete goal doing things on their own. So they understand the highle goal and autonomously work towards them. For example, if I give the same migration task to an agentic AI, this is how it will behave. It will first understand the high level goal which is to deploy a microser from VM to Kubernetes. Then create a plan with 10 or 50 subtask. Spin up specialized agent for specific task and then use different tools like GitHub, Docker, Cubectl, Terapform etc. If there are any issues, it will also fix it on their own. Let's say if the deployment is failed, it will also roll back to the previous version. It will monitor the rollout for stability. It will also update the documentation to to include all the operation that it has done. Create a PR in GitHub and also notify you on Slack when everything is done. So, agent AI does not just complete task, it runs operation. It will update documentation for you. It will create pull requests.

title: Generative AI vs AI Agents vs Agentic AI Explained Simply with Example in 5 Mins!
text: It will notify on its own and that's why it is called as fully autonomous. So, in short, use Gen AI tools to create content or code files. Use AI agents for single specific task and use agentic AI for long complex operations. I hope this video was informative. title: Learn AI terms in 60 seconds! #part1
text: Let's understand AI buzzwords. MCP or Model Context Protocol is a standardized protocol that lets AI models securely connect to external tools and services like GitHub, Slack, Notion, databases, APIs, and lot more without custom integrations. RAG or Retrieval Augmented Generation is a way to give AI access to your own documents and data, so it answers questions based on your information rather than just using the data that it has been trained on. Context window is the maximum amount of information an AI model can process and remember one time during a conversation, which also includes prompts, conversation history, and retrieve files. Multimodal AI, so AI system that can understand and generate multiple types of data including text, video, audio, PDFs, and structured document in a single workflow. Comment below AI for part two. title: NemoClaw by Nvidia Explained in 60 seconds! Openclaw vs nemoclaw
text: What is NVIDIA Nemo Guard? So, recently Open Guard, an AI agent framework, became the fastest growing open source project in history. But, enterprises still blocked it on day one due to security concerns. Why? Because Open Guard had no proper sandboxing, no auditing, and no way to control what an AI agent could access. In a real environment, one compromised agent can take over your entire system. And to solve this, NVIDIA launched Nemo Guard. So, Nemo Guard is a security layer that wraps Open Guard without changing how agents are built. Using Nemo Guard, every AI agent now runs in a sandbox container, and all network access is blocked by default. You can define exactly what each agent is allowed to do using a simple YAML policy file, and the model is deployed locally on your infrastructure, so the data never leaves unless you choose to send it. So, the idea is simple. Use Open Guard to build your AI agents, and use Nemo Guard to run them securely in production. Subscribe.

title: Everything you need to know about AWS Cloud Practitioner ☁️ #aws
text: AWS Cloud Practitioner is a foundational level certification in Amazon Web Services platform. Now, if you're someone who has experience with the cloud and have worked in the cloud for years, you can choose to skip this Practitioner certification and go for the Associate level certifications. But, as Practitioner is very easy, and if you pass it, you get 50% off for your next certification, I would recommend you doing it. The jobs you can expect after getting this certification mostly include sales and marketing jobs in cloud domain or non-technical jobs, as this is a very foundational level certification. But, you can also get entry-level jobs in some companies.

title: Authentication vs Authorization Explained in 1 min! #devops #software
text: Let's understand the difference between authentication and authorization. Authentication. Authentication is a process of verifying users identity. Who are you? Are you the right person trying to access this application or system? So for example, whenever you log into your AWS account with your right username and password, you are authenticated which means you are the right person with correct credentials to access this AWS account. On the other hand, authorization is about checking what you can access or what permissions do you have in the system. For example, in your AWS account, the admins or root user are authorized to access everything. Whereas database admins are only authorized to use RDS or a particular service. In short, authentication is confirming who you are by checking your credentials. And authorization means what you can do by checking your permissions. Subscribe.

title: Docker Sandbox for AI Agents Explained!
text: Running AI agents on your machine can be risky because they can execute commands, install packages, and modify files directly. And that's why Docker AI sandboxes exist. So, Docker AI sandbox is a secure environment that runs your AI agent in an isolated micro VM instead of your local system. Let me explain how this actually works. So, each sandbox gets its own file system, network stack, and Docker engine. So, the AI thinks that it is running on a full machine, but everything is actually contained inside this isolated environment. Docker sandboxes uses five isolation layer: hypervisor, network, Docker engine, workspace, and credential proxy. These layers ensure that the agent cannot access your host system files or sensitive data. So, the agent can build, run, and test code freely inside the sandbox. And once the task is done, you can simply stop or delete the sandbox, and everything else will be wiped.

title: What is Kubernetes Operator and How it works? #kubernetes
text: What is a Kubernetes operator? So a Kubernetes operator is an extension of Kubernetes that lets you manage complex application in the same way as you manage pods or deployments. So how it actually works is you need a custom resource definition in which you define your new object which could be a posgress cluster or a Prometheus instance. Along with this you also need a controller that is going to continuously check this objects to make sure that it matches the desired state. For example, you can use Postgress operator to create and manage Postgress SQL clusters just by defining Postgress cluster resource in the CRD. Similarly, you can also use Prometheus operator to manage and deploy Prometheus instances in the cluster and so on. So, an operator is just a CRD with a controller. Subscribe.

title: What is Forward Deployed Engineer role? What Does a FDE Actually Do? #tech #ai
text: Forward deployed engineer or FDE is one of the highest paid roles in tech today with companies like Google, Nvidia, OpenAI hiring aggressively. So, what exactly does a forward deployed engineer do? So, most engineers work in their companies and build products for their own users, but FDE does the opposite. They go directly into customers environment and make things work there. So, if a large enterprise buys an AI product, FDE is usually the engineer that will help them deploy it in real world. So, things like understanding clients existing system, integrating everything together, and making sure that it runs in real production system. Everyday work for an FDE could be setting up infrastructure on AWS, writing scripts to integrate APIs, deploying AI agents, building rack pipelines or automation workflow, or maybe debugging a Kubernetes cluster. To land an FDE role, you need to have hands-on experience with technologies like Kubernetes, REST API, cloud platforms like AWS or Azure, even Python, vector databases, automation tools like N8N, or even LLM frameworks like LangChain. title: What is mlOps? MLOps explained simply in 60 seconds! #mlops
text: What is MLOps? MLOps is basically DevOps for machine learning. In DevOps, you automate building and deploying of software. In MLOps, you automate building, deploying and managing machine learning models. This is how MLOps actually work. First step is to version control everything, your code, your data, and machine learning models using tools like MLflow. Doing this, we can keep track of any changes happening in the training data and we can also retrain our models anytime we want. Next, we will build pipelines to automate all this process from training a model to testing it and deploying it without any manual work using tools like CubeFlow. For deployment, you can package your models into a Docker container and run them on Kubernetes. Once the model is live, you can also monitor it using tools like Prometheus. And finally, if you want to scale the entire system, you can use cloud GPUs, autoscaling or optimized infrastructure. Comment below MLOps if you want a complete video with the project. Subscribe.

title: Every Kubernetes Object Explained in Just 5 minutes!
text: Every Kubernetes cluster consists of so many different objects and it is super important for you to understand them. So in this video I'm going to explain you every cubernetes object. So make sure you watch this video till the end. Let's go. Starting with pod. The smallest and the most basic object is a pod which runs one or more containers. Containers inside a pod share the same network and storage. Pods are temporary which means if it fails it might get restarted or replaced losing all the pod data. And that's why you normally don't use pods by themselves in production. To run pods more reliably, Kubernetes has controllers. A deployment is the most common controller. Deployment makes sure that the right number of pods are running, supports scaling up and down, and also allows rolling updates and roll backs. Underneath a deployment is a replica set. A replica set maintains a specified number of pod replicas by automatically creating or deleting the pods as needed. For application that needs stable storage or identity like

title: Every Kubernetes Object Explained in Just 5 minutes!
text: databases, you can use stateful set. Stateful sets provide stable network identities, persistent storage and order deployments which is critical for databases or message cues. For tasks that need to run on every node, such as log collection or monitoring agents, there's demon set. Demon sets ensure that specific pods run on every node or selected nodes. If you need to run something once and then stop, you can use a job. Jobs in Kubernetes are used to run pods that perform finite task and terminate when completed. And if you want to run a job on a schedule like chron job in Linux, you can use a chron job object. Now configuration is managed separately from code. In Kubernetes, config maps store non-sensitive data like app configuration while secrets store sensitive data such as password or API keys. For storage, Kubernetes uses persistent volumes to represent actual disc space either in cloud or physical volumes. Use persistent volume claims to let pod request disk space on these volumes. A storage class defines different types of storage like SSDs or

title: Every Kubernetes Object Explained in Just 5 minutes!
text: slower disk and allow Kubernetes to automatically provide storage as needed. Networking is another important piece of the cluster. Service expose pods by giving them permanent IP and DNS name. So even if pods get replaced, apps can still talk to each other. Services are of different types. For example, cluster IP which is internal to the cluster and other service types are node port, load balancer and external link. Ingress. Ingress resources manage HTTP and HTTPS traffic routing requests to services based on host names or paths. Network policies. Network policies act as a firewall controlling which pods or namespace can communicate with each other. For security and access control, Kubernetes uses arbback or role-based access controls. Service account is used by pod to access the Kubernetes API. Roles and cluster roles define what actions are allowed and role bindings or clustal bindings assign those permissions to the user or pods. To control resources, resource kotas limit how much CPU, memory or storage a namespace can use while limit ranges set default or maximum values for pods. Pod

title: Every Kubernetes Object Explained in Just 5 minutes!
text: level security like blocking privileged containers or forcing non-root users is handled with pod security admissions. At the cluster level, name spaces can be used to provide logical separation, allowing multiple teams or applications to share a cluster safely. Node. Nodes are physical or virtual machine that actually run the pods. Kubernetes also supports automatic scaling. The horizontal pod autoscaler changes the number of pods based on CPU memory or custom metrics. The vertical pod autoscaler can adjust resources like CPU memory requested by the pods. The cluster autoscaler works at the node level adding or removing machines depending on the workload. Custom resource definitions. Kubernetes can be extended through custom resource definitions.
